title: How did Aussie builder collapse with more than $3billion debt
text:
By SARAH BROOKES - SENIOR REPORTER, AUSTRALIA and KYLIE STEVENS, SENIOR BREAKING NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  00:57 AEST, 26 August 2026   |  Updated:  02:06 AEST, 26 August 2026

66

View  comments

How does a major property developer collapse during a housing shortage?

That's the question confronting thousands of would-be homeowners after Sydney-based Bathla Group entered voluntary administration with an estimated $3.6billion in liabilities, leaving up to 15,000 homes and 500 jobs hanging in the balance.

The developer, which built its reputation delivering budget-friendly housing across Sydney's booming north-west, blamed a combination of weakening sales, rising construction costs and tighter lending conditions for its downfall.

In an Instagram post, Bathla Group managing director Bhart Bhushan described the company's financial troubles as the result of a 'perfect storm' of softening sales, tax changes and escalating building costs.

'These changes in market conditions have had flow-on effects to lending markets, putting further pressure on the business,' he said.

The warning signs were already flashing

Days before the company collapsed, NSW regulators fined Bathla and imposed stricter licence conditions over insurance lapses following months of complaints from purchasers left waiting on delayed projects.

The action came amid growing concern about financial pressures across the construction sector as developers grapple with supply chain delays, higher costs, tighter margins and weaker demand from investors.

Bathla Group builds budget-friendly housing estates, townhouses and apartments across Sydney

Bathla Group managing director Bhart Bhushan (pictured) cited a 'perfect storm' of softening sales, tax change impacts, and higher construction costs

Up to 15,000 homes that were under construction are now under a cloud of uncertainty

Housing Industry Association NSW executive director Brad Armitage said the industry is experiencing difficult conditions that mean many projects, especially in Western Sydney, are not feasible.

'Margins are beginning to recover but recent federal budget tax changes on the back of multiple rate rises means that market confidence is at an all-time low,' he told the Daily Mail.

'This is leading to more uncertainty in builders' and developers' pipelines... this means investment starts to go elsewhere, with many builders looking to commercial building work or even other investments altogether.'

Mr Armitage said while finance and lending conditions are making it harder for developers to bring projects to market or complete existing developments, it was tax settings, including the Foreign Investor surcharge and recent capital gains and negative gearing changes, which were having a much bigger impact.

'The housing industry has been calling for more support to make projects 'stack up' for years, so everybody already knew all of the issues contributing to this before today,' he said.

'What hasn't been looked at seriously is the enormous cost of infrastructure being heaped on new home buyers, though the entire community benefits, and without a drastic change, entry-level housing first home buyers can afford, will continue to be difficult to deliver.'

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed Bathla's collapse was due to the mounting pressures facing the residential construction sector, with developers squeezed by rising interest rates, soaring construction costs, project delays and a slowdown in new-home sales.

Mr Oliver said insolvencies among developers had remained elevated since the pandemic, warning the industry was still grappling with many of the same challenges that triggered a wave of collapses several years ago.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver (pictured) said Bathla's collapse reflected the mounting pressures facing the residential construction sector

'Property developers and home builders are getting hit from all angles: higher interest rates, higher costs, delays in completing things, more regulation and, more recently, a decline in new home sales,' he said.

Bathla's downfall appears to have been fuelled in part by its reliance on private-credit lenders. Traditional banks grew increasingly cautious about funding residential developments amid rising costs and weaker market conditions.

Mr Oliver said banks became more reluctant to lend to the sector because projects were riskier, pushing some developers towards private-credit providers who were willing to take on greater risk in exchange for higher returns.

'If the banks won't lend them any more, often they've got to issue debt that is taken up by these private credit funds,' he said.

'Private credit funds tend to be a more risky investment than a corporate bond fund.'

Mr Oliver said large corporate collapses often appeared to come out of nowhere because publicly acknowledging financial distress could trigger an immediate loss of sales and funding.

'If they were out there saying, ''It looks like we may not make it'', that would make life even more difficult for them, because home sales would dry up and any new loans they need would be harder to get,' he said.

Far-reaching impacts

Despite Australia's housing shortage, Mr Oliver said many projects were no longer stacking up financially, with developers facing higher interest rates on top of the rising construction expenses and falling demand for newly built homes.

Bathla's website claims its broader development pipeline includes 22,000 apartment dwellings and a further 3,500 homes highlighting the enormous scale of the collapse

'The collapse highlights the uncomfortable reality that even during a housing shortage, developers can fail when construction costs, borrowing costs and weak sales make projects unviable,' he said.

The failure also highlights the growing difficulty of meeting the federal government's target of building 1.2 million new homes over five years.

'We're running way below target already,' Mr Oliver said, noting housing completions have been falling well short of the pace required to meet the goal.

Bathla formally entered voluntary administration on Tuesday, with restructuring firm Teneo appointed to assess the group's finances and attempt to stabilise operations.

While administrators have estimated up to 15,000 homes could be affected, Bathla's website claims its broader development pipeline includes 22,000 apartment dwellings and a further 3,500 homes, highlighting the enormous scale of the collapse and the potential impact on buyers, subcontractors and lenders.

Teneo's Stephen Longley said urgent discussions with lenders were underway.

'Our priority is to stabilise the business so that construction activity and property settlements can continue in the ordinary course,' he said.

'Our objective is to ensure project continuity wherever practicable and work with lenders to minimise disruption for employees, customers and contractors.'

Mr Bhushan said appointing administrators was the best way to protect stakeholders and maximise the chances of completing thousands of homes amid Australia's ongoing housing crisis.

The company's main entity, Universal Property Group, owes almost $3.2billion, while related building arm Raj & Jai Construction carried liabilities of about $304million at the end of the 2024-25 financial year.
